beats.narration_text: Hej. This is Liam, in for Bear. This film is about why multiplying two matrices in the other order gives a different answer: a matrix is a move, not a number, and two moves in the other order land somewhere else. By the end you'll see it on a grid. The trap is treating AB like three times four.

props.question: Why does the order you multiply two matrices in change the answer?
lines: A matrix is a move, not a number — two moves in the other order land somewhere else.
You will see it on a grid: follow where the two basis arrows go.
The trap: treating AB like 3 × 4. Order only drops out in one special case.
props.heading: What This Film Is About

beats.narration_text: Why should you care? Every rotation, every neural-network layer, every camera move is matrices applied in order. Get the order wrong and the picture is wrong, silently — no error, just a different answer. See a matrix as a move, and the rule for composing them stops being a formula to memorize.

learn.question: Same two boxes of numbers, multiplied both ways — why two different answers?
learn.action: Show A·B and B·A computed on screen; both boxes fill; they differ.

learn.inference: The numbers can't explain it; something about what a matrix IS must.
learn.next_question: What does a 2×2 box of numbers actually do?

beats.narration_text: Two boxes of numbers. Multiply them this way, you get one answer. Multiply them the other way — a different one. Both computations are correct. So the arithmetic isn't the story.

learn.question: What does a box of numbers do?
learn.action: Put a grid on screen; apply A: watch the basis arrows and the whole grid move.
learn.observation: Grid lines stay parallel and evenly spaced; the two basis arrows land on A's columns.
learn.inference: A matrix is a move of the plane, recorded by where the basis arrows land.
learn.next_question: Does the second box do the same kind of thing?

beats.narration_text: Put the numbers away and put a grid down. Watch the two basis arrows — the ones every other arrow is built from — when A acts. They land exactly on A's columns. The whole grid follows them.

beats.motion_claim: apply_matrix is the concept: the grid moving IS what a matrix is.

learn.question: Is B a move too?
learn.action: Reset the grid; apply B; the arrows land on B's columns.
learn.observation: Same rule, different move — a shear instead of a rotation.
learn.inference: Every matrix is a move; the columns are the record.

beats.narration_text: Same grid, now B. Different move — a shear — same rule: the arrows land on B's columns. Two matrices, two moves. So what does it mean to multiply two moves?

learn.question: Can't we just multiply the numbers and read the answer?
learn.action: Compute AB entry by entry with the dot-product rule, slowly.
learn.observation: Eight multiplications, four sums. It produces a box. It says nothing about why.
learn.inference: The rule is a recipe for the record, not an explanation of the move.
learn.next_question: What if we followed the arrows instead?

beats.narration_text: The obvious thing — the thing the chapter's rule tells you — is to multiply the numbers. Row times column, eight products, four sums. Here's the box. It's right. And it tells you nothing about why the other order is different.

shot.visual_intent: Row-times-column: a row of A and a column of B highlight in turn, products appear, sum into an entry of AB; the finished box sits there; a dim caption: 'correct — and mute'.

show.event: row 1 of A and column 1 of B highlight; products write

beats.motion_claim: The natural attempt walked to its limit: the box appears and explains nothing.

learn.question: What if we followed the arrows instead of the numbers?
learn.action: Reframe: 'AB' means do B first, then A. Put the grid back. Before it moves: predict where the red arrow ends.
learn.observation: The viewer commits to a landing spot.
learn.inference: The representation is the grid; multiplication is 'follow the moves in order'.

beats.narration_text: Here's the reframe. A B doesn't mean a number times a number. It means: do B, then A. Follow the arrow. Before it moves — commit. Where does the terracotta arrow land if we shear first, then rotate?

learn.question: Where does the arrow land, both ways?
learn.action: Shear then rotate — the arrow lands. Reset. Rotate then shear — it lands somewhere else.
learn.observation: Two different landing spots for the same two moves.
learn.inference: Order changes the destination; that is all AB ≠ BA ever meant.
learn.next_question: Can we say that in general?

learn.question: Can we say this in general?
learn.action: The two landing spots become the two boxes from the HOOK; the equation (AB)v = A(Bv) writes beside the arrow it describes.
learn.observation: The box is the record of the landing; the equation says 'apply B, then A'.
learn.inference: Matrix multiplication is composition of moves, and composition is not commutative.
learn.next_question: What does each symbol in that line mean?

beats.narration_text: This thing we keep pointing at deserves a name. Multiplying matrices is composing moves — and composing is not commutative. The two boxes from the start were the two landing spots all along.

shot.visual_intent: The two landing arrows ReplacementTransform into the AB and BA boxes from B11; MathTex (AB)\vec v = A(B\vec v) writes beside the arrow; the word 'composition' lands in serif as the name.

learn.action: Equation persists on the MAIN side; zones write into the SIDE band: LHS/RHS as sentences, the '=' as a claim, the glossary with roles, one worked value.

learn.inference: The notation is a description of what was watched.

beats.narration_text: Read the line. Left side: the combined move, applied to the arrow. Right side: B's move, then A's move, one after the other. The equals sign is a promise — those are the same arrow. v is the arrow; A and B are moves; the parentheses are the order.

shot.visual_intent: Split stage: the MathTex equation persists left; right band writes LHS sentence, RHS sentence, '= : the same arrow', then a three-row glossary (v · arrow · the input; A, B · moves · what acts; ( ) · order · which first); the symbol being explained highlights terracotta in the equation and its row at once.

beats.narration_text: Back to the start. Two boxes, two answers — because two orders, two landings. The entries that disagreed are the coordinates of two different places. What this film did not do: tell you when order does NOT matter. That's your turn.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A matrix is a move, recorded by where the basis arrows land. Multiplying matrices is doing one move after another. Doing them in the other order lands somewhere else — that is all A B is not B A ever meant. The row-times-column rule is correct and mute; the grid is where the reason lives.

artifactLines: A matrix is a move; its columns record where the basis arrows land.
Multiplying matrices is composing moves, one after another.
The other order lands somewhere else — AB ≠ BA is just that.
Row-times-column is correct and mute; the grid holds the reason.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Give me two 2×2 matrices that DO commute, and two that don't. For each pair, describe both matrices as moves of the plane, then predict — before computing — whether AB equals BA, and say why in terms of the moves. Then compute both products and check. What do the commuting pairs have in common as moves? Look for two things in the answer: did it predict from the moves before touching the numbers, and did it name the geometric reason, not just 'the entries match'.
